tagline.text: An unexpected piece of Africa where you feed giraffes on a Palawan island

children.text: A wildlife sanctuary on an island north of Busuanga, where giraffes and zebras brought over from Kenya in
still roam freely today. You can even get up close to the endangered Calamian deer, making it a great change of pace for a day trip during a Coron holiday.

Calauit Safari Park (formally the Calauit Game Preserve and Wildlife Sanctuary) is a roughly 3,700-hectare wildlife reserve covering all of Calauit Island, just across a narrow strait from the northwestern tip of Busuanga Island in the Calamian Islands of northern Palawan. It was established by presidential decree under the Marcos government in
, when, between 1976 and
, eight species of African animals — giraffes, zebras, elands, impalas, waterbucks, gazelles, topis, and bushbucks, 104 animals in all — were shipped in by boat from Kenya and released here.

At the time, Kenya was struggling to protect its wildlife amid drought and poaching, and the Philippines presented this as an international conservation project. Over the decades, many species failed to adapt to the climate and environment and died out, but giraffes and zebras have bred across several generations and still roam the island's grasslands today. As of around
, the park is home to about 20 giraffes and around 30 zebras.

The park also plays an important role in conserving species native to the Philippines. The Calamian deer, found only in the Calamian Islands, has grown from around 25 animals at the start of the conservation project to more than 1,000, and the park also protects the Philippine crocodile, Palawan bearded pig, binturong (bearcat), and Philippine mouse-deer. It has been managed by the Palawan provincial government since

If a Coron trip is usually built around lakes, limestone islands, and wreck diving, Calauit offers a completely different experience. Getting close enough to feed a giraffe from your hand in the early morning is a moment that stays with adults and children alike. It's a great choice for family travellers, animal lovers, or anyone who wants a day of rest between sea-based itineraries.

If you time your visit for the morning feeding, a keeper will hand you a bundle of leaves so you can feed the giraffes yourself. You'll get to watch, right up close, as a giraffe curls its long tongue around the leaves to pull them in.
Ride an open-top truck or jeepney across the grasslands in search of herds of zebra and deer. This usually comes with an extra fee (around
This small, shy native deer gathers in herds along the edge of the grassland and the forest line. Approach quietly and you can spot dozens at once.
Visit the enclosures for native species — the Philippine crocodile, binturong, porcupine, Palawan bearded pig — with a guide's commentary.
The trip begins with a short bangka crossing of about
5–10 minutes
from Makalachao Pier at the northwestern tip of the main island of Busuanga to Calauit Island. On clear days the water is an emerald green.
Many Calauit tours are packaged together with a visit to the pure white sandbar beach of nearby Ditaytayan Island. A morning safari followed by an afternoon swim makes for a full day.

Within Coron town, a single tricycle ride costs about

The dry season, from
November
to
May
, is the best time to visit. During this period, the roads in northern Busuanga are in good condition and the sea is calm, making the wharf crossing easy.
December–February
is especially cool, making even a midday safari bearable. From March to
May
, it's hot and the grasslands turn a dry gold, making the landscape look even more like an African savanna.
From
June
to
October

, the southwest monsoon brings frequent rain, and unpaved sections can turn muddy, lengthening travel times. The Calamian Islands can fall within typhoon paths some years, so it's essential to check the forecast between July and
November

Most travellers stay in Coron town and visit Calauit as a day trip. Coron town has everything from guesthouses at around
a night to mid-range hotels in the

range, and it's also convenient for reaching Maquinit Hot Spring or the Mount Tapyas viewpoint. If you'd prefer somewhere quieter, you can also spend a night or two in northern Busuanga or at an island resort, in which case meals are usually taken care of at the resort.

There are no proper restaurants inside the park, so check whether lunch is included in your tour, or, if travelling independently, bring a packed lunch and water from Coron town. In Coron town, you can enjoy cashews (a Palawan specialty), coconut crab (a protected species best avoided), fresh grilled fish and kinilaw, and mango shakes made with Busuanga mangoes. Seafood restaurants near the market let you pick items by weight and have them cooked to order.
Giraffe feeding usually happens in the morning, so choose as early a tour as possible.
Most of the trip is spent in a vehicle, so motion sickness medication and a neck pillow help. Some stretches of road are still bumpy and winding.
There's no shade on top of a safari truck, so a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen are essential.
A giraffe's long tongue may touch your hand when you feed it, so bring wet wipes, and a wide-angle lens works better than a telephoto for close-up giraffe photos.
Coron town has ATMs, but there are none in northern Busuanga or inside the park, so bring cash for the entrance fee and tips.
When booking a joiner tour, check carefully whether the entrance fee, truck fee, lunch, and Ditaytayan Island entrance fee are included, to avoid extra costs on the day.
If travelling with children, pack plenty of snacks and water given the long drive.

Rather than scheduling Calauit right after arriving in Coron, it works well as a rest-day activity between lake and lagoon hopping tours. Since Calauit involves little time on the water, it's also easier on companions prone to seasickness.
Deer and zebras are sensitive to noise. When you get off the truck to observe them, avoid loud noises and move slowly to get a longer, closer look.
Giraffes and zebras are close to their wild state. Don't approach or stand behind them in places the keepers haven't permitted — zebras in particular can deliver a dangerous kick.
Feeding the animals snacks or human food other than what the keepers provide is prohibited.
The park's entrance fee and operating hours (generally
8 AM–5 PM
) can change under provincial government policy, so check the latest notice.
During the rainy season, flooded roads and suspended boat service can lead to tour cancellations. Build a spare day into your Coron itinerary.
Mosquitoes can be plentiful, so bring insect repellent and long sleeves.
